paragraphs: Dimension reduction methods turn complex data into a smaller representation by trying to preserve relationships between observations. Popular methods such as t-SNE and UMAP compare pairwise similarities in the original and reduced spaces. This paper asks what statistical model could explain those objectives and help clarify which relationships they preserve poorly.

The authors introduce a framework built around hidden graphs in both spaces. These graphs describe dependencies among observations through a Markov random field, and cross entropy connects the two graph models. Particular choices of graph priors recover existing methods based on pairwise similarities. This gives several familiar algorithms a common probabilistic interpretation rather than treating their objectives as unrelated constructions.

The framework also exposes a statistical degeneracy in the methods that use shift-invariant kernels. The authors connect this degeneracy to poor preservation of coarse relationships across the data. They additionally show that PCA fits into the framework as a graph coupling model without this degeneracy. The contribution is therefore both a unification of methods and an explanation of a specific weakness in part of that family.
neurips-2022-a-probabilistic-graph-coupl.tldr: A probabilistic framework unifies similarity-based dimension reduction and reveals a statistical degeneracy linked to poor preservation of coarse relationships.

paragraphs: When two variables contain categories rather than numerical measurements, determining which one causes the other calls for a model suited to that data. This paper addresses that two-variable causal discovery problem. Its starting point is a new classifier called classification with optimal label permutation, or COLP, which becomes the building block for a causal model.

COLP is designed to be parsimonious: it represents the classification relationship with a compact model. The authors show that this design produces a causal model whose direction is provably identifiable. To learn the direction, their algorithm fits the causal and reverse-direction models and compares their likelihoods. The identifiability result concerns this proposed model, rather than an unrestricted ability to infer causation from any pair of categorical variables.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show favorable performance compared with leading existing methods. The authors also provide an R package containing the algorithm and a benchmark collection of categorical cause-effect pairs. Together, the model and software make the contribution both theoretical and usable: the paper explains why directional information can exist within its model and supplies a straightforward procedure for extracting it.
neurips-2022-bivariate-causal-discovery-.tldr: COLP uses a compact classification model to make causal direction identifiable for categorical variable pairs and learns it by comparing directional likelihoods.

paragraphs: Many generative models create samples by passing a standard Gaussian random input through a deterministic neural network. This paper studies how well these push-forward models can represent distributions with multiple separated modes. Such modes correspond to distinct concentrations of data, so fitting them requires reproducing both the concentrations and their separation.

The authors prove that accurate fitting requires a sufficiently large Lipschitz constant, which measures how strongly the network can amplify changes in its input. They derive lower bounds on distribution mismatch, measured by total variation distance and Kullback-Leibler divergence, that depend on both mode separation and this constant. These bounds connect a restriction on the generating network directly to limits on the distributions it can approximate.

This matters because restricting Lipschitz constants is commonly used to stabilize generative training. The results establish a trade-off between that stabilization strategy and the ability to fit multimodal data. Experiments on one-dimensional and image datasets support the analysis. The authors also empirically find that diffusion models avoid this limitation in their evaluations; that observation is distinct from the formal bounds proved for the studied push-forward models.
neurips-2022-can-push-forward-generative.tldr: Push-forward generators face a provable trade-off between Lipschitz-based stabilization and accurately representing separated modes.

paragraphs: Data from different environments often follow different distributions. Although these changes complicate ordinary learning, they can also reveal causal structure that a single stable distribution leaves ambiguous. This paper investigates when environmental changes provide enough information to distinguish causal graphs that would otherwise belong to the same observational equivalence class.

The central assumption is the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis: a distribution changes because only a small number of causal conditional relationships change. The authors introduce the Mechanism Shift Score, or MSS, to use this pattern when comparing candidate causal structures. The approach supports different empirical estimators and is nonparametric, while explicitly exploiting the sparsity of changes across environments.

Under the sparse mechanism shift hypothesis, the authors prove that MSS identifies the complete causal structure with high probability. This guarantee depends on structured changes; the paper does not claim that arbitrary environmental changes make causal discovery possible. Experiments verify behavior predicted by the theory and compare estimators and score functions. The resulting perspective treats certain distribution shifts as informative evidence about causation, with a concrete scoring method for using that evidence.
neurips-2022-causal-discovery-in-heterog.tldr: MSS uses sparse changes in causal mechanisms across environments to identify causal structure with high probability under the stated hypothesis.

paragraphs: Proving that neural network training reaches zero loss often involves assumptions about network size or the amount of training data. This paper develops a proof strategy that reaches beyond analyses requiring infinitely many parameters or finitely many samples. It studies gradient flow, the continuous-time formulation of following the negative loss gradient.

The strategy centers on Rayleigh quotients and uses them to establish Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz inequalities. These inequalities connect the geometry of the loss to the progress made by gradient flow, providing a route to convergence proofs. The authors show that the Rayleigh quotient perspective also brings several existing convergence analysis techniques into a common framework.

The paper applies this strategy to various examples of parametric learning and a broader collection of architectures and loss functions. Because the analysis need not assume a finite sample set, it can extend to minimizing test loss as well as training loss. These are convergence results for the examples and settings covered by the analysis, rather than a guarantee for every network. The contribution expands the mathematical tools available for studying learning beyond the over-parameterized regime.
neurips-2022-convergence-beyond-the-over.tldr: Rayleigh quotients provide a unified route to gradient-flow convergence proofs without requiring infinite parameter counts or finite sample sets.

paragraphs: Estimating misinformation's influence requires more than observing that people who encounter it behave differently. The paper addresses the distinction between association and causal influence, with particular attention to social media activity unfolding over time. It aims to estimate effects at the individual level while handling data at a larger scale than small psychological experiments.

The authors build a causal framework using temporal point processes, which model the timing of events. Their estimation method combines a neural temporal point process with Gaussian mixture models to estimate individual treatment effects. The temporal formulation makes event sequences central to the analysis, while the proposed combination is designed to make the estimates both efficient and precise on large datasets.

Synthetic-data experiments support the method's effectiveness and efficiency. The authors then apply it to posts and engagement concerning COVID-19 vaccines. In that application, the model identifies a causal effect of misinformation associated with more negative subjective emotions toward vaccines. This is a finding from the model's analysis of that dataset; its stated outcome concerns emotional attitudes rather than a demonstrated change in vaccination behavior.
neurips-2022-counterfactual-neural-tempo.tldr: A causal model of social media event timing estimates individual misinformation effects and finds negative effects on vaccine-related emotions in its real-data application.

paragraphs: Curriculum reinforcement learning trains an agent through a sequence of tasks that moves toward a difficult target. This paper asks how to define that progression when the starting and target tasks are distributions rather than single tasks. Its guiding idea is to divide a potentially large distribution shift into smaller, more manageable stages.

The proposed method, GRADIENT, formulates curriculum construction as an optimal transport problem. It uses a contextual distance that depends on the tasks and builds intermediate distributions through geodesic interpolation, expressed using Wasserstein barycenters. This gives the progression a mathematical structure: each stage occupies an intermediate position between the source and target under the chosen task distance.

GRADIENT handles nonparametric distributions with either continuous or discrete contexts. The authors prove smooth transfer between successive stages under specified conditions, so that guarantee is conditional rather than automatic for every curriculum. In locomotion and manipulation experiments, the method improves both learning efficiency and eventual performance relative to the evaluated baselines. The contribution connects a principled way of measuring task movement with a practical procedure for generating training stages.
neurips-2022-curriculum-reinforcement-le.tldr: GRADIENT constructs reinforcement learning curricula through optimal transport between task distributions, with conditional transfer guarantees and improved experimental performance.

paragraphs: Estimating an intervention's effect from observational data becomes difficult when unobserved factors influence the relationships being studied. Sometimes images or text contain indirect information about these missing confounders. This paper develops a way to use that information for causal effect estimation, bringing unstructured inputs into a task often based on more conventional variables.

The proposed deep multi-modal structural equations form a generative model. Confounders appear as latent variables, while the available unstructured inputs serve as proxies that carry information about them. The model supports multiple proxies across modalities, including images and text, and accommodates missing data. This setup explicitly represents the distinction between a hidden confounder and an observed signal that only indirectly describes it.

Experiments in genomics and healthcare show that the approach uses unstructured inputs to correct for confounding and outperforms the evaluated propensity-score methods. These findings support the argument that proxy information can improve causal effect estimates. The broader possibility is to make previously unused data useful for causal analysis, with the images and text contributing information about missing variables rather than being treated as direct observations of those variables.
neurips-2022-deep-multi-modal-structural.tldr: A multimodal generative causal model uses images and text as proxies for hidden confounders, improving effect estimation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A vision model can perform well on familiar data yet struggle when the test distribution changes. Combining models can help, and weight averaging offers a way to combine them into one network. This paper proposes Diverse Weight Averaging, or DiWA, with the aim of increasing the diversity of the functions represented by the models being averaged.

DiWA averages weights from independent training runs. Differences in hyperparameters and training procedures produce more functional diversity than collecting models along one training run. To explain why this matters, the authors decompose expected error into bias, variance, covariance, and locality terms. This analysis connects weight averaging with the more familiar practice of combining models' predictions.

The decomposition indicates that weight averaging succeeds when the variance term dominates, a situation the authors show arises when the marginal distribution changes at test time. On the DomainBed benchmark, DiWA consistently improves the reported state of the art without adding inference overhead. The empirical result supports using diversity across training runs to strengthen a single averaged model's behavior under distribution shift.
neurips-2022-diverse-weight-averaging-fo.tldr: DiWA averages weights from diverse independent training runs to improve distribution-shift generalization without extra inference overhead.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to partial differential equations can approximate an individual solution or learn a solution operator that maps problem inputs to solutions. Physics-informed approaches additionally incorporate the governing equations. This paper develops a general mathematical framework for bounding approximation error across these related architectures, including PINNs, DeepONets, FNOs, and physics-informed operator models.

The framework builds on existing neural network approximation results and carries them into the more involved architectures used for differential equations. This matters because a result about a basic network does not by itself establish how accurately an entire solution-learning architecture can represent its target. The authors provide a common route from those existing results to rigorous bounds for these larger constructions.

They use the framework to derive what they describe as the first rigorous approximation-error bounds for physics-informed operator learning. They also show that the covered architectures mitigate the curse of dimensionality when approximating nonlinear parabolic equations. The guarantees concern efficient approximation of solutions or solution operators. Their significance is to establish representational accuracy mathematically, rather than to assert that every training procedure will find the corresponding approximation.
neurips-2022-generic-bounds-on-the-appro.tldr: A general framework derives rigorous approximation bounds for physics-informed and operator-learning networks, including results that mitigate dimensionality costs for nonlinear parabolic PDEs.

paragraphs: Removing noise from a learning problem does not necessarily make it computationally easy. This paper proves superpolynomial lower bounds for learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks with Gaussian inputs in the noise-free setting. The main result applies to statistical query algorithms, a learning model that obtains information through statistical queries about the data.

Previous lower bounds for ReLU learning either involved adversarial noise or applied to more restricted query models. A prior result also ruled out general statistical query lower bounds for real-valued function families satisfying a particular non-degeneracy condition. The authors overcome this obstacle by refining a lifting procedure that transfers Boolean PAC learning problems into problems with Gaussian inputs.

The improved reduction extends to other learning models and is more efficient in many studied cases. It yields additional cryptographic hardness results for PAC learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks, along with membership-query lower bounds for constant-depth networks. These findings identify difficulty within precise computational models and assumptions. They show that noiseless labels alone do not remove the theoretical barriers established for these network-learning problems.
neurips-2022-hardness-of-noise-free-lear.tldr: The paper proves superpolynomial statistical-query lower bounds for learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks even with Gaussian inputs and no label noise.

paragraphs: Image reconstruction often uses regularizers to favor properties such as sparsity, low rank, or smoothness. Non-convex regularizers can improve reconstruction quality, but their optimization analyses commonly guarantee only convergence to a critical point. That leaves a gap between reaching a point where optimization stops and reaching the best value of the reconstruction objective.

This paper addresses that gap through invex regularization. The authors provide a collection of regularizers with proved invexity and establish convergence to global optima for various reconstruction techniques equipped with them. The role of invexity is to support stronger optimization guarantees while retaining regularization choices intended to improve reconstructed images.

Numerical experiments across several imaging tasks and benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed regularization. The authors describe their work as the first practical application of invex regularizers to imaging with global-optimum guarantees. The contribution combines a mathematical property of the regularizers, convergence results for the corresponding reconstruction methods, and empirical evaluation. Those guarantees apply to the analyzed constructions rather than to non-convex regularization in general.
neurips-2022-improved-imaging-by-invex-r.tldr: Proved invex regularizers improve image reconstruction while enabling global-optimum convergence guarantees for the analyzed methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering the parameters of a single-layer ReLU network from samples of its output distribution when some samples are arbitrary outliers. The target parameters are the weight matrix and bias vector. The analysis assumes non-negative biases and that the fraction of genuine samples, denoted by p, is greater than two thirds.

The method combines gradient descent with filters based on either a median or a trimmed mean. These filters mitigate the influence of corrupted samples during parameter estimation. This connects an ordinary optimization procedure with robust filtering, allowing the authors to analyze recovery even though the outliers themselves need not follow a specified distribution.

For parameter error ε, the authors prove that sample counts scaling as 1/p² + 1/(ε²p) are sufficient, ignoring logarithmic factors. The sufficient running time has the same dependence multiplied by d², where d is the problem dimension. These are upper bounds under the stated assumptions, rather than claims that every algorithm requires those resources. Theory and simulations together describe how contamination, desired accuracy, and dimension affect the studied recovery procedure.
neurips-2022-learning-distributions-gene.tldr: Gradient descent with robust filters recovers single-layer ReLU parameters under arbitrary outliers, with proved resource bounds when biases are non-negative and over two thirds of samples are genuine.

paragraphs: Learning tasks one after another creates a practical problem: a model can lose earlier knowledge as it learns new concepts. Storing old data or repeatedly training a large model may be too expensive. This paper addresses continual learning in the increasingly common setting where practitioners begin with a pretrained Transformer instead of training a network from scratch.

The proposed method extends pretrained Transformers with Adapters and trains incrementally across a sequence of tasks. Its design supports information sharing between tasks while scaling to many tasks without significant overhead. The important resource goal is to avoid making the model continually larger as the task sequence grows, while still allowing it to acquire new capabilities.

Experiments on image and text classification show that the method maintains good predictive performance without retraining the model or increasing its parameter count over time. The resulting model also performs inference significantly faster than the compared leading Adapter-based methods. These findings support a practical combination of continued learning, bounded model size, and faster prediction across the evaluated task sequences.
neurips-2022-memory-efficient-continual-.tldr: A Transformer-and-Adapter method learns successive tasks with a fixed parameter count, shared information, and faster inference in image and text experiments.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines optimization across devices whose datasets can differ substantially. FedProx is a distributed proximal optimization method used in this setting, but its theoretical explanation has relied on restrictive assumptions about how local objectives differ. Existing results also focused on smooth objectives, leaving a gap between the method's practical use and the situations covered by theory.

This paper develops a convergence analysis for FedProx and a minibatch stochastic extension through algorithmic stability. The resulting guarantees do not depend on certain stringent local dissimilarity conditions. They also cover non-smooth federated optimization problems, expanding the kinds of objectives for which favorable complexity results can be established.

For the analyzed non-convex problems, the theory additionally gives linear speedups with minibatch size and the number of sampled devices. This connects greater participation and larger batches to improved theoretical efficiency. The result is not that heterogeneity or smoothness never matters; it is that the particular dissimilarity restrictions and smoothness assumptions addressed by the paper are unnecessary for obtaining its favorable FedProx bounds.
neurips-2022-on-convergence-of-fedprox-l.tldr: A stability-based analysis gives FedProx convergence guarantees beyond restrictive local-dissimilarity and smoothness assumptions, plus linear minibatch and device speedups.

paragraphs: Posterior sampling uses uncertainty about an environment to guide reinforcement learning decisions. This paper proposes an optimistic variant, OPSRL, for episodic tabular Markov decision processes whose dynamics can depend on the step within an episode. The setting has H steps per episode, S states, A actions, and T episodes of interaction.

OPSRL needs only logarithmically many posterior samples in H, S, A, and T for each state-action pair. The authors prove a high-probability regret bound scaling as the square root of H³SAT, apart from logarithmic factors. Regret measures the cumulative cost of learning instead of acting optimally, so the bound describes how that cost grows with interaction and problem size.

The proof relies on a sharp anti-concentration inequality for linear combinations of a Dirichlet random vector, extending an earlier normal-approximation result for Beta distributions. This technical result supports the optimistic sampling analysis and may have separate uses. The regret dependence matches the stated lower bound up to logarithmic factors, resolving the cited open questions for the episodic setting while keeping posterior sampling requirements small.
neurips-2022-optimistic-posterior-sampli.tldr: OPSRL achieves high-probability regret matching the stated lower-bound scaling up to logarithmic factors while requiring only logarithmically many posterior samples.

paragraphs: Predictive coding can reduce communication costs by subtracting predictable information from incoming signals. But producing and transmitting predictions also consumes resources and introduces noise. This paper develops a theory that accounts for costs in both feedforward and feedback communication, along with noise throughout the computation, to ask when predictive feedback is actually useful.

The authors formulate inference as message-passing on a graph, with feedback acting as an internal control signal. The objective balances accurate tracking of a hidden state against computational cost. They analyze a scalar hidden state in a linear dynamical system with Gaussian variability, providing a specific setting in which the best feedback strategy can be studied.

Architectural constraints affect that strategy. In particular, Dale's law can make feedforward and feedback costs asymmetric because each neuron has exclusively excitatory or inhibitory outgoing connections. Under such constraints, the theory predicts feedback strength and how feedback enters inference. Optimal strength varies non-monotonically with computational parameters and world dynamics, producing transitions between regimes where feedback helps and regimes where it offers no utility.
neurips-2022-phase-transitions-in-when-f.tldr: A cost-and-noise-aware theory of inference predicts transitions in whether feedback is useful, depending on architecture, computation, and world dynamics.

paragraphs: Gaussian process inference becomes expensive as datasets grow, making approximations common. Those approximations introduce error in addition to the uncertainty caused by limited observations. This paper argues that using an approximate posterior without accounting for computational uncertainty leaves out a consequential part of what the model does not know.

The authors develop a class of methods that consistently estimates uncertainty from both finite data and finite computation. Common approaches based on Cholesky factorization, conjugate gradients, and inducing points can be represented within this class. The framework therefore connects several existing approximation strategies to a shared treatment of the uncertainty their computation introduces.

For methods in the class, the paper proves posterior-mean convergence in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space and separates the combined covariance into mathematical and computational components. It also shows that the combined variance gives a tight worst-case bound on squared error between the estimated mean and latent function. Benchmark experiments demonstrate consequences of ignoring computational uncertainty and show improved generalization when it is implicitly modeled.
neurips-2022-posterior-and-computational.tldr: A unified Gaussian process framework accounts for uncertainty from both limited data and approximate computation, with error guarantees and empirical generalization gains.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning reduces dependence on labels by learning from relationships between samples, but comparing node instances can require substantial time and memory. Large graphs may also demand many training epochs. This paper revisits that approach after identifying what the authors describe as inappropriate sigmoid use in two representative methods, DGI and MVGRL.

The proposed alternative is Graph Group Discrimination, or GGD. It learns by distinguishing two groups of node samples using binary cross entropy, replacing the similarity-computation objective. The method also needs fewer training epochs to reach competitive performance on large datasets. Together, the simpler learning objective and shorter training explain the proposed efficiency advantage.

Experiments report better performance than leading self-supervised methods on eight datasets. On ogbn-arxiv, training takes 0.18 seconds, or 6.44 seconds including preprocessing, with a reported speed advantage exceeding 10,000 times over graph contrastive baselines and substantially lower memory use. On the billion-edge ogbn-papers100M graph, nine hours of training yields better accuracy and efficiency than the compared contrastive methods. These results demonstrate the practical scale of the proposed change in learning objective.
neurips-2022-rethinking-and-scaling-up-g.tldr: GGD replaces pairwise similarity learning with group discrimination, achieving strong graph representations with sharply reduced training time and memory in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether using curvature information can reduce the samples needed for stochastic optimization. It analyzes Stochastic Cubic Regularized Newton, or SCRN, on functions satisfying gradient dominance with a parameter between one and two. This property ensures that every first-order stationary point is a global optimum, giving the analysis a route from optimization progress to global accuracy.

The authors prove sample-complexity bounds for reaching an ε-accurate global optimum, with different rates depending on the gradient-dominance parameter. These improve the best-known bounds for stochastic gradient descent. They also obtain the same improvement under a weaker gradient-dominance condition applicable to policy-based reinforcement learning, extending the comparison to stochastic policy gradient methods.

For the case where the parameter equals one, variance reduction with changing batch sizes reduces the stated average sample complexity to order ε⁻². This is an average-complexity result, distinct from the earlier total sample bounds. Experiments in several reinforcement learning settings show strong SCRN performance relative to first-order methods. The contribution combines conditional theoretical sample savings with empirical evidence that curvature-based updates can be useful in the evaluated learning problems.
neurips-2022-stochastic-second-order-met.tldr: Under gradient-dominance conditions, stochastic cubic-regularized Newton improves known sample-complexity bounds over stochastic gradient methods.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can learn effective TCP congestion-control policies, but neural policies are difficult to interpret and can be cumbersome to run in constrained networking environments. This paper proposes a two-stage process: first learn a neural policy, then distill its behavior into lightweight symbolic expressions that are easier to understand and implement.

The central technique is symbolic branching. It produces a symbolic tree whose rules account for different network conditions, allowing the distilled controller to respond to context. This gives the symbolic policy a way to express conditional decisions while retaining a simpler representation than the original neural network. The aim is to preserve learned decision quality in a more accessible form.

Evaluations in simulation and emulation show that the symbolic rules preserve, and often improve, performance relative to the compared leading neural policies. They are also faster and simpler than a standard neural network. These findings support symbolic distillation as a practical route from a learned controller to deployable rules, while the stated evidence concerns the tested environments rather than a universal reliability guarantee.
neurips-2022-symbolic-distillation-for-l.tldr: Symbolic branching distills learned TCP controllers into interpretable rules that preserve or improve tested performance while running faster.

paragraphs: Survival analysis predicts how long it will take for an event to occur. In a dynamic setting, that prediction can use a sequence of changing states rather than a single observation. This paper asks how relationships between successive states can improve learning of the distribution over event times.

The authors develop discrete-time survival algorithms inspired by temporal-difference learning. Their central condition is temporal consistency: predictions from consecutive states should align after accounting for the time that passed between them. This gives the learning procedure a relationship to exploit across the sequence, beyond directly fitting each prediction to an observed survival outcome.

The method can be combined with any parametric survival model and naturally handles right-censored observations, where observation ends before the event is seen. Empirical comparisons show better sample efficiency and predictive performance than approaches that directly regress observed outcomes. The findings indicate that temporal relationships can supply useful learning structure: the sequence contributes through consistency between neighboring predictions as well as through the recorded event information.
neurips-2022-temporally-consistent-survi.tldr: Enforcing consistency between successive survival predictions improves sample efficiency and prediction in experiments while accommodating censored observations.

paragraphs: At initialization, a feedforward network's logits are conditionally Gaussian given a random covariance matrix determined by its penultimate layer. Understanding that matrix helps describe the network's initial outputs. This paper studies its distribution when both depth and width grow, focusing on activation shaping that prevents the covariance from becoming degenerate.

Analyses based on infinite width can overlook small random changes from one layer to the next. In very deep networks, those changes accumulate. The authors therefore study a joint infinite-depth-and-width limit and identify the precise activation scaling needed for a nontrivial limiting process. They show that the covariance evolves according to a stochastic differential equation, which they call the Neural Covariance SDE.

Simulations show that this equation closely matches covariance distributions in finite networks. The authors also recover a necessary-and-sufficient condition, based on the activation function, for exploding and vanishing norms in large shaped networks. The contribution makes accumulated randomness part of the description of initialization, providing a richer account than one that discards layer-level fluctuations before considering large depth.
neurips-2022-the-neural-covariance-sde-s.tldr: A stochastic differential equation describes covariance fluctuations at initialization when shaped networks grow jointly in depth and width.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can be straightforward to train while remaining difficult to control in terms of generalization and adversarial robustness. Singular values of convolutional layers influence these properties, making them useful targets for intervention. Existing control methods, however, can be computationally impractical or rely on coarse approximations of the quantities they seek to manage.

This paper proposes a tensor-train-based representation of convolutional layers. It retains control over the actual singular values of the convolutional mappings while introducing structured sparsity and a hardware-friendly form. The authors describe the trade-off as an insignificant reduction in layer expressivity in exchange for easing the computational constraints of previous approaches.

The method is evaluated in modern convolutional networks, with analysis of model performance, calibration, and adversarial robustness. The authors report improved network properties with their construction. The contribution is a practical connection between a mathematically relevant layer property and an implementable representation: singular-value control becomes part of the layer's structure, rather than relying only on expensive computation or coarse estimation.
neurips-2022-towards-practical-control-o.tldr: A tensor-train representation makes actual convolutional singular values controllable in a hardware-friendly form with a stated small expressivity trade-off.

paragraphs: Learning curves reveal how well a reinforcement learning policy performs, but say less about how its internal function changes. ReLU policies divide their input space into regions within which their behavior is linear. This paper tracks the number and density of those regions across continuous-control tasks and policy network sizes to examine how policy complexity evolves.

A natural expectation is that training creates denser regions around frequently visited states, enabling finer control. The authors test this idea using different trajectory-based viewpoints. Along fixed trajectories produced by the final policy, region density increases only moderately during training. Along the policy's current trajectories, density decreases because those trajectories also grow longer as learning proceeds.

These observations show why the reference trajectory matters when interpreting changes in region density. The findings suggest that the complexity of learned control policies does not principally arise from a large increase in the complexity of functions encountered on and around their trajectories. This is an empirical interpretation grounded in the measured regions, offering a different view of learning progress from performance curves alone.
neurips-2022-understanding-the-evolution.tldr: Trajectory-based measurements suggest that deep reinforcement learning policy complexity does not mainly grow through a large increase in local linear-region density.
